rewrite.explanation: A delay is a threshold: the callback becomes eligible after that much time and actually runs when the loop next reaches the timers phase, so the real delay is at least what you asked for and often more. Node is single-threaded, so a synchronous block, a slow callback or a busy poll phase pushes every pending timer out — and a delay under 1 ms is clamped up to 1 ms rather than being exact. Never build a clock, a rate limit or a deadline out of accumulated setTimeout calls: read Date.now() or process.hrtime.bigint() when the callback actually runs.

rationale: Correct and directly useful for timeouts and scheduling under load; the defect is two nonsense options plus a hint and explanation that do no teaching.
evidence: node (Node 22.22.2): setTimeout(fn, 50) behind a 120 ms synchronous block fired after 125.9 ms

defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback

options: Cancels the timer
Stops the timer from keeping the process alive
Makes the timer fire sooner than its delay
Releases the callback so it can be garbage collected
rewrite.hint: A pending timer is one of the reasons Node has not exited yet. Ask what changes about that reason, rather than about when the callback fires.
rewrite.explanation: Node keeps running while any referenced handle is outstanding, and a pending timer is one. unref() drops that reference: the callback still fires normally if the loop is alive when the delay elapses, but if the timer is the only thing left the process exits instead of waiting for it. It does not cancel the timer — that is clearTimeout — does not change the delay, and has nothing to do with garbage collection. Use it for background work such as a periodic health ping that should never hold a CLI or worker open; ref() restores the reference.

rationale: unref is the standard fix for a process that will not exit, and the ref/unref idea carries over to sockets and servers; only the option set and the filler hint hold it back.
evidence: node (Node 22.22.2): setTimeout(...,200).unref() -> the process exited immediately with code 0 and the callback never ran; the same timer without unref kept the process alive and fired at 200 ms

options: A callback in the next timers phase, like setTimeout(fn, 0)
A microtask, run after the current operation and before the loop continues
A callback in the check phase, like setImmediate(fn)

rewrite.hint: It shares a queue with something you already use every day. Ask when a .then callback runs relative to the code that scheduled it.
rewrite.explanation: queueMicrotask(fn) puts fn on the same microtask queue promise reactions use, so it runs as soon as the current synchronous operation finishes and always before the loop moves on to timers, I/O or check callbacks — which is exactly why it is not the same as setTimeout(fn, 0) or setImmediate(fn), both of which wait for a loop phase. It is how you defer work by one turn without allocating a promise, and unlike process.nextTick it does not cut ahead of promise callbacks. Nothing here involves a thread: microtasks run on the same thread as the rest of your code.

rationale: The key is right and the microtask/phase boundary is genuinely worth understanding at this level, but the options mix spec jargon with nonsense and the explanation contrasts nothing.
evidence: node (Node 22.22.2): sync, then Promise.then and queueMicrotask, then nextTick, then setImmediate, then the 0 ms timer — the queueMicrotask callback ran with the promise reactions and before any loop phase

rewrite.hint: Three of these create concurrency inside your own program. Ask which one can launch a binary that was never written in Node.
rewrite.explanation: child_process starts a separate operating-system process running any program — git, ffmpeg, a shell command or another Node script — and hands you its stdio and exit code. cluster also creates processes, but only copies of your own Node app sharing a listening socket, and worker_threads runs your JavaScript on threads inside the same process; neither can launch an external binary. net is the TCP module and starts no process at all.

objective: Know what child_process.exec does: run a command string through a shell and buffer all output for the callback.
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback

rewrite.hint: The name says how the command is run, not how its output comes back. Ask which of these needs a shell to interpret the string you passed.
rewrite.explanation: exec hands the whole command string to a shell (/bin/sh on Unix, cmd.exe on Windows), so pipes, globs, quoting and && all work, then collects everything the child printed and passes the complete stdout and stderr to the callback as strings once it exits. Both consequences matter: the output is held in memory, and any user input interpolated into that string can inject extra commands — pass arguments as an array to execFile or spawn when the input is not yours. Streaming without a shell is spawn, running another Node script over an IPC channel is fork, and no thread is involved in any of them.

rationale: Choosing exec over spawn is a decision with security and memory consequences, and the key is right; the explanation currently stops at the definition.
evidence: node (Node 22.22.2): exec("echo hi && echo $0") ran through a shell (stdout contained "/bin/sh") and delivered stdout to the callback as a string

rewrite.hint: Picture a command that prints a gigabyte, and a command string assembled from user input. Ask which of the two survives both situations.
rewrite.explanation: spawn returns a ChildProcess whose stdout and stderr are readable streams, so output is processed as it arrives and its size does not matter; exec waits for the child to exit and hands you one string. spawn also executes the file directly with no shell, and arguments are passed as an array that is never re-interpreted: spawn("echo", ["*.mjs"]) prints the literal *.mjs, and a shell string such as "echo a && echo b" fails with ENOENT unless you pass { shell: true }. That is what makes spawn the safe default for anything built from user input. It is asynchronous and returns a ChildProcess rather than a promise — the blocking forms are spawnSync and execSync.

rationale: A correct key on the choice that decides both memory behaviour and injection exposure; the length clue and a non-teaching explanation are the defects.

options: A new thread inside the current process

rewrite.hint: The name is borrowed from POSIX, but Node’s version does not duplicate the running program. Ask what it starts, and what the two ends can then do.
rewrite.explanation: child_process.fork(modulePath) is spawn specialised for Node: it starts a brand-new node process running the module you name — fresh memory, its own event loop, a different pid — and wires up an IPC channel so parent and child can exchange messages. Despite the name it is not POSIX fork(2): none of the parent’s memory is copied and the child begins at the first line of your module. It is not a thread either (that is worker_threads, which shares the process) and it does not go through a shell (that is exec).

rationale: A supported API with real use (cluster is built on it) and a correct key, but the option set leaves out the POSIX-fork confusion that the name invites.
evidence: node (Node 22.22.2): fork("child.cjs") returned a ChildProcess with connected === true, a send() method and a pid different from the parent, while worker_threads.isMainThread stayed true in both

options: Shared variables — both processes see the same objects

rewrite.hint: Two processes have separate memory, so nothing can be handed over by reference. Ask what form the data has to take to cross between them.
rewrite.explanation: A forked child has its own memory, so the two sides exchange copies: the parent calls child.send(value), the child calls process.send(value), and each side receives the other’s messages through a "message" event — process.on("message") in the child, child.on("message") in the parent. Values are serialised, so functions and class instances do not survive the trip and mutating the object you sent changes nothing on the other side. Shared variables and global state cannot reach across a process boundary at all, and while argv can carry startup data it is one-way and fixed at launch.

rationale: Message passing versus shared memory is a durable concurrency lesson and the mechanism is right, but the keyed option names only the child-side API and two distractors repeat one another.
evidence: node (Node 22.22.2): parent fork + child.send({hello:"from parent"}) -> the child’s process.on("message") fired and its process.send reply arrived at the parent’s "message" event with a different pid

options: The command runs twice

rewrite.hint: exec keeps everything the child prints until it exits. Ask what has to give when that pile outgrows the limit Node puts on it.
rewrite.explanation: exec holds all of stdout and stderr in memory until the child exits, bounded by the maxBuffer option, which defaults to 1 MiB. When the child writes past it Node terminates the child and calls your callback with an error whose code is ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER — it does not truncate silently and it does not spill to a file, so a command that behaves in testing starts failing once a log or a directory listing grows. Raising maxBuffer only moves the ceiling; for output of unknown size use spawn and read the stream as it arrives.

rationale: A production failure mode that appears only under real data, with a correct key; three of the four options are noise and the explanation gives neither the limit nor the fix.
evidence: node (Node 22.22.2): exec of a child writing 3 MiB returned err.code "ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER", message "stdout maxBuffer length exceeded"; the same command with {maxBuffer: 8*1024*1024} succeeded with 3145728 bytes
